topic: Google SRE book ch. 21 Handling Overload
claim: Google caps each request at three attempts; after three failures the error goes up to the caller.
quote: First, we implement a per-request retry budget of up to three attempts. If a request has already failed three times, we let the failure bubble up to the caller.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 21 Handling Overload, written by Alejandro Forero Cuervo, edited by Sarah Chavis (Google, O'Reilly)

topic: Google SRE book ch. 21 Handling Overload
claim: Each client keeps retries below 10% of its requests; combined with the 3-attempt cap this limits worst-case growth from about 3x to about 1.1x.
quote: Each client keeps track of the ratio of requests that correspond to retries. A request will only be retried as long as this ratio is below 10%.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 21 Handling Overload, Alejandro Forero Cuervo
note: Also: 'layering on the per-client retry budget (a 10% retry ratio) reduces the growth to just 1.1x in the general case -- a significant improvement.' (em-dash replaced in this note). Third mechanism: a retry counter in request metadata.

topic: Google SRE book ch. 21 Handling Overload
claim: Client-side adaptive throttling rejects new requests locally with probability max(0, (requests - K x accepts) / (requests + 1)), counting over the last two minutes, with K usually 2.
quote: max(0, (requests - K × accepts) / (requests + 1))
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 21 Handling Overload, Alejandro Forero Cuervo
note: The equation 'Client request rejection probability' is an image; transcribed from it (fraction written inline; x is the multiplication sign U+00D7). Text: 'each client task keeps the following information for the last two minutes of its history' and 'We generally prefer the 2x multiplier.'

topic: Google SRE book ch. 21 Handling Overload
claim: Clients send freely until requests reach K times accepts; lowering K (for example to 1.1) throttles more aggressively, and Google prefers K = 2.
quote: Clients can continue to issue requests to the backend until requests is K times as large as accepts.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 21 Handling Overload, Alejandro Forero Cuervo
note: Also: 'Reducing the modifier to 1.1 means only one request will be rejected by the backend for every 10 requests accepted.'

topic: Google SRE book ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures
claim: Retrying at several layers multiplies attempts, so retries should live at one deliberately chosen level.
quote: avoid amplifying retries by issuing retries at multiple levels: a single request at the highest layer may produce a number of attempts as large as the product of the number of attempts at each layer to the lowest layer.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures, written by Mike Ulrich
note: Preceding sentence: 'Think about the service holistically and decide if you really need to perform retries at a given level.'

topic: Google SRE book ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures
claim: Ch. 22 suggests a server-wide retry budget, for example 60 retries per minute per process, beyond which requests simply fail.
quote: Consider having a server-wide retry budget. For example, only allow 60 retries per minute in a process, and if the retry budget is exceeded, don't retry; just fail the request.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures, Mike Ulrich
note: Curly apostrophe normalised. Preceded by 'Limit retries per request. Don't retry a given request indefinitely.'

topic: Google SRE book ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures
claim: For steady traffic, queues should be small relative to the thread pool (50% or less) so the server rejects early instead of building latency.
quote: it is usually better to have small queue lengths relative to the thread pool size (e.g., 50% or less), which results in the server rejecting requests early when it can't sustain the rate of incoming requests.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures, Mike Ulrich
note: Curly apostrophe normalised. Context: with 100 ms per request a full queue makes a request take 1.1 seconds; 'Gmail often uses queueless servers'.

topic: Google SRE book ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures
claim: With deadline propagation the frontend sets one absolute deadline and every downstream RPC inherits the remaining time (30 s, minus 7 s, gives B a 23 s deadline).
quote: With deadline propagation, a deadline is set high in the stack (e.g., in the frontend). The tree of RPCs emanating from an initial request will all have the same absolute deadline.
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures, Mike Ulrich
note: Example: 'if server A selects a 30-second deadline, and processes the request for 7 seconds before sending an RPC to server B, the RPC from A to B will have a 23-second deadline.'

topic: Google SRE book ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures
claim: Chapter 22 opens with two epigraphs about exponential backoff and jitter.
quote: If at first you don't succeed, back off exponentially. Dan Sandler, Google Software Engineer Why do people always forget that you need to add a little jitter? Ade Oshineye, Google Developer Advocate
source: Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 22 Addressing Cascading Failures, Mike Ulrich

topic: The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)
claim: If one request in 100 takes 1 s on a server, a user request fanning out to 100 such servers is slower than 1 s 63% of the time (1 - 0.99^100).
quote: If a user request must collect responses from 100 such servers in parallel, then 63% of user requests will take more than one second
source: The Tail at Scale, Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, Communications of the ACM 56(2)
note: cacm.acm.org returned 403; text from the PDF on Barroso's site (page footer 'february 2013 | vol. 56 | no. 2'). Setup: 'a 99th-percentile latency of one second ... one user request in 100 will be slow (one second).' Also: 2,000 servers with 1-in-10,000 slow gives 'almost one in five user requests taking more than one second'.

topic: The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)
claim: A cheap hedging variant sends the backup request only after the first has been outstanding longer than the 95th-percentile expected latency, adding about 5% load.
quote: One such approach is to defer sending a secondary request until the first request has been outstanding for more than the 95th-percentile expected latency for this class of requests.
source: The Tail at Scale, Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, Communications of the ACM 56(2)
note: The PDF text is interrupted by a pull-quote between 'until the first' and 'request has been'; joined here. Next: 'This approach limits the additional load to approximately 5% while substantially shortening the latency tail.'

topic: The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)
claim: In a Google BigTable benchmark reading 1,000 keys across 100 servers, a hedge after a 10 ms delay cut 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with 2% more requests.
quote: sending a hedging request after a 10ms delay reduces the 99.9th-percentile latency for retrieving all 1,000 values from 1,800ms to 74ms while sending just 2% more requests.
source: The Tail at Scale, Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, Communications of the ACM 56(2)
note: Note the benchmark hedges after a fixed 10 ms delay, not 'after the 95th percentile'; the two are described separately in the paper. Setup: 'reads the values for 1,000 keys stored in a BigTable table distributed across 100 different servers'.

topic: Metastable failures (Bronson et al., HotOS 2021)
claim: A metastable failure is a bad, low-goodput state entered via a trigger that persists after the trigger is removed because a sustaining effect keeps the system there.
quote: Metastable failures occur in open systems with an uncontrolled source of load where a trigger causes the system to enter a bad state that persists even when the trigger is removed.
source: Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems, Nathan Bronson, Abutalib Aghayev, Aleksey Charapko, Timothy Zhu, HotOS '21
note: Next: 'In this state the goodput (i.e., throughput of useful work) is unusably low, and there is a sustaining effect -- often involving work amplification or decreased overall efficiency -- that prevents the system from leaving the bad state.' em-dash replaced.

topic: Metastable failures (Bronson et al., HotOS 2021)
claim: Above an invisible load threshold a system moves from stable to vulnerable: still healthy, but a trigger can tip it into the metastable state; many systems run vulnerable all the time for efficiency.
quote: Once the load rises above a certain threshold -- implicit and invisible -- the system enters a vulnerable state. The vulnerable system is healthy, but may fall into an unrecoverable metastable state due to a trigger.
source: Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems, Bronson, Aghayev, Charapko, Zhu, HotOS '21
note: em-dash replaced. Also: 'many production systems choose to run in the vulnerable state all the time because it has much higher efficiency than the stable state.'

topic: Metastable failures (Bronson et al., HotOS 2021)
claim: Outages are usually blamed on the trigger, but the true root cause of a metastable failure is the sustaining effect.
quote: It is common for an outage that involves a metastable failure to be initially blamed on the trigger, but the true root cause is the sustaining effect.
source: Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems, Bronson, Aghayev, Charapko, Zhu, HotOS '21

topic: Metastable failures (Bronson et al., HotOS 2021)
claim: Retries are one of the most common sustaining effects; in the paper's example a web app with one retry after 1 s sends 560 QPS instead of 280 once database latency rises, and stays stuck after a 10 s network outage.
quote: One of the most common failure-sustaining mechanisms is request retries.
source: Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems, Bronson, Aghayev, Charapko, Zhu, HotOS '21
note: Example text: 'A user request to the web application results in one query to the database and another retry query if the first query does not return in 1 s.' and 'So long as latency is high, client queries will continue at 560 QPS due to retries.' Figure 2: stable below 150 QPS, vulnerable above.

topic: Metastable failures in the wild (Huang et al., OSDI 2022)
claim: The OSDI 2022 study examined public incident reports: its abstract reports 22 metastable failures from 11 organizations, and at least 4 of 15 major AWS outages in a decade were metastable.
quote: First, metastable failures are universally observed -- we present an in-depth study of 22 metastable failures from 11 different organizations.
source: Metastable Failures in the Wild, Lexiang Huang, Matthew Magnusson, Abishek Bangalore Muralikrishna, Salman Estyak, Rebecca Isaacs, Abutalib Aghayev, Timothy Zhu, Aleksey Charapko, OSDI '22
note: em-dash replaced. Inconsistency in the paper: section 2 says 'We identify 21 metastable failures (Table 1)'. Abstract also: 'at least 4 out of 15 major outages in the last decade at Amazon Web Services were caused by metastable failures.'

topic: Metastable failures in the wild (Huang et al., OSDI 2022)
claim: The retry policy is by far the most common sustaining effect, in more than 50% of the studied incidents (11 named incidents); load shedding was the most common mitigation, also in over 50%.
quote: By far, the most common sustaining effect is due to the retry policy, affecting more than 50% of the studied incidents
source: Metastable Failures in the Wild, Huang et al., OSDI '22
note: Continues: 'GGL2, GGL3, AWS1, AWS2, AWS3, AZR2, AZR4, IBM1, SPF1, SPF2, and CAS2 incidents are all sustained by retries.' (11 incidents). Also: 'Around 45% of observed triggers in Table 1 are due to engineer errors' and 'Load shedding was the most popular mitigation effort used in over 50% of the incidents.'

topic: Gray failure (Huang et al., HotOS 2017)
claim: Gray failure's key feature is differential observability: failure detectors see the system as healthy while applications are being hurt.
quote: We also argue that a key feature of gray failure is differential observability: that the system's failure detectors may not notice problems even when applications are afflicted by them.
source: Gray Failure: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud-Scale Systems, Peng Huang, Chuanxiong Guo, Lidong Zhou, Jacob R. Lorch, Yingnong Dang, Murali Chintalapati, Randolph Yao, HotOS '17
note: Curly apostrophe normalised. Formal definition: 'a system is defined to experience gray failure when at least one app makes the observation that system is unhealthy, but observer observes that system is healthy.' Same PDF also at https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/paper-1.pdf.

topic: Python: tenacity
claim: The current tenacity release on PyPI is 9.1.4 (uploaded 2026-02-07).
source: tenacity on PyPI (JSON API)
note: Quote is the info.version field.

topic: Python: tenacity
claim: wait_random_exponential(multiplier=1, max=MAX_WAIT, exp_base=2, min=0) waits uniform(min, min(multiplier * exp_base**(attempt-1), max)), which tenacity documents as AWS Full Jitter.
quote: corresponds to the "Full Jitter" algorithm described in this blog post: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/
source: tenacity/wait.py at tag 9.1.4, jd/tenacity
note: Signature is inherited from wait_exponential: multiplier=1, max=_utils.MAX_WAIT, exp_base=2, min=0. Docstring example: wait_random_exponential(multiplier=0.5, max=60). Implementation: return random.uniform(self.min, high).

topic: Python: tenacity
claim: In tenacity 9.1.4, wait_exponential_jitter(initial=1, max=MAX_WAIT, exp_base=2, jitter=1) waits min(initial * 2**n + uniform(0, jitter), max), following Google Cloud Storage's retry strategy.
quote: The wait time is min(initial * 2**n + random.uniform(0, jitter), maximum)
source: tenacity/wait.py at tag 9.1.4, jd/tenacity
note: The main branch (unreleased as of fetch) adds min and multiplier and deprecates initial: 'The wait time is max(min, min(multiplier * 2**n + random.uniform(0, jitter), maximum))'. Docstring links https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/retry-strategy.

topic: Python: httpx
claim: httpx enforces timeouts by default: a TimeoutException after 5 seconds of network inactivity, split into connect, read, write and pool timeouts.
quote: HTTPX is careful to enforce timeouts everywhere by default. The default behavior is to raise a TimeoutException after 5 seconds of network inactivity.
source: Timeouts, HTTPX documentation
note: Also: 'There are four different types of timeouts that may occur. These are connect, read, write, and pool timeouts.' Example: timeout = httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=60.0).

topic: Python: requests
claim: requests has no default timeout, and its docs say nearly all production code should pass one.
quote: Nearly all production code should use this parameter in nearly all requests. Failure to do so can cause your program to hang indefinitely
source: Quickstart (Timeouts), Requests documentation
note: Advanced page (https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/): 'By default, requests do not time out unless a timeout value is set explicitly. Without a timeout, your code may hang for minutes or more.'
